questions.stem: The CI job runs `claude "Review this PR for bugs"` and hangs until it times out after 60 minutes. What is the fix?

options.text: Run Claude Code non-interactively with `-p` (`--print`), for example `claude -p "Review this PR for bugs"`.
options.why: Print mode runs once and exits, which is what CI needs.

options.text: Set the environment variable `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=1`.
options.why: This isn't a real Claude Code setting.

options.text: Add `--batch` to the command.
options.why: This flag doesn't exist.

options.text: Pipe `yes` into the command to auto-answer prompts.
options.why: That is a hack that doesn't address interactive mode.

questions.explanation: `-p`/`--print` is the non-interactive mode for scripts and CI. Watch out for made-up flags among the distractors.

questions.stem: A downstream script posts findings as inline PR comments and needs reliably parseable output with fields `file`, `line`, `severity` and `message`. What should the CI invocation use?

options.text: `claude -p ... --output-format json --json-schema <schema>` so the output is machine-readable and conforms to the expected structure.
options.why: Structured output flags make CI output reliably parseable.

options.text: Ask in the prompt for "a nicely formatted list" and parse it with regex.
options.why: This is brittle.

options.text: Use `--output-format text` and split on newlines.
options.why: That is unstructured.

options.text: Write the output to CLAUDE.md and read it back.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is for memory, not an output channel.

questions.explanation: In CI, combine `-p` with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` to get structured, validated output.

questions.stem: The CI reviewer re-posts the same 12 findings on every push to a PR, and developers are annoyed. What is the best fix?

options.text: Include the previous run's findings (or the existing PR comments) in the prompt and instruct the reviewer to report only new or still-unresolved issues.
options.why: Supplying prior findings avoids duplicate reports.

options.text: Run the review only once per PR.
options.why: New pushes would go unreviewed.

options.text: Lower the model temperature.
options.why: That doesn't prevent repeats.

options.text: Delete all previous bot comments before each run.
options.why: This loses history and still spams notifications.

questions.explanation: Give CI reviewers the prior findings so that they report only what is new.

questions.stem: The test-generation step keeps suggesting tests that already exist in the repo. What should change?

options.text: Provide the existing relevant test files (or a summary of the existing test coverage) as context, and ask for tests only for uncovered behaviour.
options.why: The model can't avoid duplicating tests it hasn't seen.

options.text: Ask the model to "be creative".
options.why: That leads to irrelevant tests, not avoided duplicates.

options.text: Generate tests in a random order.
options.why: This makes no difference.

options.text: Limit the generator to 3 tests per PR.
options.why: The tests would still be duplicates, just fewer of them.

questions.explanation: Provide existing tests as context to avoid duplicate test suggestions.

questions.stem: In the same CI job, Claude generates a fix for a failing test and then reviews its own fix before auto-committing. The reviews almost always approve. What is the architectural problem?

options.text: The generating session keeps its own reasoning and is biased toward approving it. Use an independent reviewer instance (a fresh context without the generation history).
options.why: Independent review instances catch issues that self-review misses.

options.text: The review prompt is too short.
options.why: The bias comes from shared context, not prompt length.

options.text: Reviews should use extended thinking in the same session.
options.why: The same context means the same blind spots.

options.text: The reviewer should run before the generator.
options.why: That is nonsensical.

questions.explanation: Self-review is weak because the model retains its generation reasoning. Use separate instances for review.

questions.stem: CI runs of Claude Code don't follow the repo's conventions (error-handling style, banned dependencies), although local sessions do. Where should these conventions live so CI picks them up?

options.text: In the project's committed CLAUDE.md (and `.claude/rules/`), which Claude Code also loads in CI runs from the checkout.
options.why: Project memory supplies context to CI invocations too.

options.text: In each developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
options.why: CI runners don't have the developers' home directories.

options.text: Only in the CI YAML as an environment variable.
options.why: This is awkward and duplicates the repo's source of truth.

options.text: Nowhere. CI runs can't use project context.
options.why: False.

questions.explanation: Committed project CLAUDE.md gives CI runs the same project context as local runs.

questions.stem: Developers ignore the bot because about 60% of its comments are style nits or false positives. The current prompt says "Be conservative and only report important issues." What is the most effective change?

options.text: Replace the vague instruction with explicit categorical criteria: what counts as a reportable issue (for example security, correctness, data loss) and what to exclude (formatting and naming handled by linters), with concrete examples of each.
options.why: Explicit criteria reduce false positives more reliably than vague caution.

options.text: Add "only report findings you're 90% confident about".
options.why: Confidence filtering relies on poorly calibrated self-assessment.

options.text: Limit the bot to 3 comments per PR.
options.why: It might drop real security findings while keeping nits.

options.text: Switch to a larger model.
options.why: It doesn't fix the specification problem.

questions.explanation: Specific, categorical criteria beat "be conservative" or confidence thresholds for precision.

questions.stem: Most of the false positives come from one category, "possible performance issue". Security findings are accurate and valued. What is the best immediate step while the criteria are improved?

options.text: Temporarily disable the noisy performance category so trust recovers, while refining its criteria and examples offline.
options.why: False positives erode trust in all findings. Removing the noisy category protects the valuable ones.

options.text: Keep everything unchanged, because developers should learn to filter.
options.why: Trust erosion leads to developers ignoring security findings too.

options.text: Disable the entire bot.
options.why: This loses the valued security findings.

options.text: Mark performance comments as "low priority" but keep posting them.
options.why: The noise remains.

questions.explanation: False positives erode trust, so temporarily disabling a noisy category is a legitimate, proportionate move.

questions.stem: The bot is inconsistent about severity: the same kind of SQL issue is "critical" in one PR and "minor" in another. What improves consistency the most?

options.text: Define each severity level with explicit criteria and concrete code examples (for example, "critical: user input concatenated into SQL").
options.why: Concrete severity definitions anchored with examples drive consistent classification.

options.text: Ask the model to assign severity randomly and average over 3 runs.
options.why: This is nonsensical and costly.

options.text: Remove severity from the output.
options.why: Severity is needed to prioritise.

options.text: Tell the model to "be consistent".
options.why: This is vague guidance.

questions.explanation: Severity criteria with concrete code examples produce consistent ratings.

questions.stem: The bot struggles with an ambiguous case: it flags the team's intentional use of `any` in generated API client files as a type-safety issue. Which technique best teaches the distinction?

options.text: Add 2–4 targeted few-shot examples that contrast acceptable patterns (generated clients) with genuine issues (hand-written code), including the reasoning for each.
options.why: Few-shot examples with reasoning are the right tool for ambiguous distinctions.

options.text: Add 50 examples covering every file type.
options.why: This bloats the prompt. A few targeted examples work better.

options.text: Exclude all TypeScript files from review.
options.why: This loses coverage.

options.text: Tell the bot "don't flag `any`".
options.why: It would then miss genuine issues in hand-written code.

questions.explanation: Use a few targeted examples (2–4) for ambiguous cases, and show the reasoning that separates acceptable patterns from real issues.

questions.stem: Findings come back in inconsistent shapes: some have line numbers, some have suggested fixes, some have neither. What is the most effective prompt-level improvement (alongside schema enforcement)?

options.text: Include few-shot examples that demonstrate the exact output format for a finding: location, issue, severity and suggested fix.
options.why: Examples demonstrating the format improve consistency.

options.text: Ask for "detailed findings".
options.why: This is vague.

options.text: Truncate long findings.
options.why: It doesn't fix missing fields.

options.text: Randomise the order of instructions in the prompt.
options.why: This makes no difference.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples should demonstrate the desired output format as well as the reasoning.

questions.stem: An engineering manager wants to move all CI usage to the Message Batches API to save 50%. This covers (a) the blocking pre-merge review on each PR and (b) the nightly technical-debt summary. What is the correct evaluation?

options.text: Use batches for (b) only. Batches can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee, so they're unsuitable for the blocking pre-merge check in (a).
options.why: Match the API to the latency requirements.

options.text: Use batches for both. 50% savings justify slower merges.
options.why: This could block merges for up to a day.

options.text: Use batches for neither, because batch results can't be matched to requests.
options.why: `custom_id` correlates results with requests.

options.text: Use batches for (a) only, because PR reviews are the most frequent.
options.why: That is the opposite of correct.

questions.explanation: The Batches API is for non-blocking, latency-tolerant jobs. Use `custom_id` to correlate results.

questions.stem: The nightly debt job submits 3,000 requests as a batch. 41 requests failed. What should the job do next?

options.text: Identify the failed requests by `custom_id` and resubmit only those.
options.why: Resubmit only the failures, correlated through `custom_id`.

options.text: Resubmit the whole batch.
options.why: This wastes cost and time on the 2,959 successes.

options.text: Ignore the failures, because 98.6% is good enough.
options.why: That leaves silent coverage gaps.

options.text: Convert the job to synchronous calls permanently.
options.why: It loses the 50% savings over a small failure rate.

questions.explanation: Batch best practices: correlate with `custom_id`, retry failures selectively, and refine prompts on a sample before full runs.

questions.stem: A 22-file PR gets a single-pass review that misses obvious bugs in some files and makes contradictory claims about others. Which restructuring is best?

options.text: Review each file (or small group of related files) in a focused local pass, then run a separate integration pass that looks at cross-file interactions.
options.why: This avoids attention dilution while still catching cross-file issues.

options.text: Use a model with a larger context window for the single pass.
options.why: A bigger window doesn't fix diluted attention.

options.text: Run the single-pass review three times and keep only findings reported 2 out of 3 times.
options.why: Consensus filtering suppresses real but intermittently detected bugs.

options.text: Ask developers to split every PR into PRs of 3 files or fewer.
options.why: This pushes the architecture problem onto developers.

questions.explanation: Multi-pass review means per-file local passes plus a cross-file integration pass.

questions.stem: The team wants to auto-post high-certainty findings and route uncertain ones to a human triage queue. Which TWO elements are needed for this routing to be trustworthy? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Have the reviewer emit a confidence value per finding as a structured field.
options.why: Per-finding confidence enables routing.

options.text: Calibrate the confidence thresholds against a labelled set of past findings (true and false positives) before relying on them.
options.why: Uncalibrated self-reported confidence is unreliable. Calibration makes it usable.

options.text: Trust the model's raw confidence as-is, because larger models are calibrated.
options.why: Raw self-reported confidence isn't reliably calibrated.

options.text: Route all findings to humans to be safe.
options.why: That defeats the goal of automation.

options.text: Ask the generator session to rate its own findings.
options.why: That brings back the self-review bias.

questions.explanation: Per-finding confidence can drive routing, but only after calibration on labelled data.

questions.stem: The CI flow has fixed, well-understood stages: lint-aware review → test-gap analysis → summary comment. Each stage's output feeds the next. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence of focused prompts, each consuming the previous stage's structured output.
options.why: Chaining suits predictable, sequential workflows.

options.text: A dynamic coordinator that decides the stages at runtime.
options.why: Adaptive decomposition adds unpredictability that a fixed pipeline doesn't need.

options.text: One prompt that does all three stages at once.
options.why: This loses focus and makes the intermediate outputs hard to validate.

options.text: A Message Batches job for each stage.
options.why: That adds latency and doesn't support the dependency between stages.

questions.explanation: Use prompt chaining for fixed, known workflows and adaptive decomposition for open-ended ones.
